english: It was a heat such as had not been known for years. Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the houses, set hard with mud, threw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, like to steam the chicks and eggs inside them alive where they lay. Still more, every field that was a field, whether hemp or millet, hung its head limply in the reek of the earth, and there was not one thing that, green as it was, was not wilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken with the closeness of these past days, though fair, hung thick and turbid in the air near the ground, and here and there mere shapes of towering cloud, like hail parched in a roasting pan, floated in lumps. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way into the threshing-yard in the blazing sun in such weather.

Strangely, one of them lay naked, on his back upon the bare ground. What was more, for some reason, his hands and his feet were wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself showed no particular sign of minding it. He was a short man, of good colour, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stood at this man's pillow, but what was inside that, too, was not to be known.
takes.label: The dry sinophile storyteller (recommended)
takes.line: First choice: learned, deadpan, and unmoved — the voice of a man retelling a Chinese record he half believes, whose erudition is real and whose sympathy is withheld until it leaks out only as physical detail. Wrong for it: chinoiserie, archaism, whimsy, or any warmth of moral feeling at the end.

english: It was a heat unknown in recent years. Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses reflected the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, likely to steam the chicks and eggs inside alive as they were. Still more, every field that was a field, whether hemp or millet, hung its head limply in the rising heat from the earth, and there was not a single thing that was not wilted, green as it stood. The sky seen above those fields, as if dazed by the humidity of these past days, was turbid and heavy with the air near the ground, for all that it was fine, and here and there floated in drops mere shapes of towering clouds, like hail parched in a roasting pan. — The story of the "wine worm" begins with three men who, in this weather, have gone deliberately out into a threshing-yard in the blazing sun.

Strangely, one of them lay stark naked on his back on the ground. What was more, for some reason his hands and feet were wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself did not look particularly troubled by it. He was short, fresh-complexioned, somehow suggestive of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a conveniently sized unglazed earthen jar stood at this man's pillow, though what was in that, too, was unknown.
takes.label: The brisk modern ironist
takes.line: Second choice: plainer and faster, letting the absurdity of the noon cure and the pedantry of the three morals read as open satire on doctors, moralists and self-help. This sharpens the schooling aside and the "Didacticism" coda, but risks settling the question the text leaves open — an ironist this brisk will sound as if he knows the monk was a fraud, and the tale's flat, sorrowful last report of fields and sickbeds would have to be played against the grain.

Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses threw back the sunlight dull as lead, and the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, like to steam the nestlings and the eggs within them alive. This honours the pseudo-documentary measures and the marvel reported as fact, but in English it easily becomes pastiche, muffles the distinctly 1916 essayistic intrusions, and could make Akutagawa's performance of learning sound like the real antiquity it is imitating.

payload.english: I

It was a heat such as had not been known for years. Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the houses, set hard with mud, threw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, like to steam the chicks and eggs inside them alive where they lay. Still more, every field that was a field, whether hemp or millet, hung its head limply in the reek of the earth, and there was not one thing that, green as it was, was not wilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken with the closeness of these past days, though fair, hung thick and turbid in the air near the ground, and here and there mere shapes of towering cloud, like hail parched in a roasting pan, floated in lumps. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way into the threshing-yard in the blazing sun in such weather.
notes: Kept the hail-parched-in-a-pan simile literal though stiff; it is bookish comparison, not to be smoothed. Kept "wine worm" as the single fixed term.

payload.english: Strangely, one of them lay naked, on his back upon the bare ground. What was more, for some reason, his hands and his feet were wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself showed no particular sign of minding it. He was a short man, of good colour, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stood at this man's pillow, but what was inside that, too, was not to be known.
notes: "thin cord" renders hosobiki; "unglazed jar" renders suyaki no kame. Left the jar's contents withheld as the Japanese does.

payload.say: Drafted p4-p6 as held tableau, keeping the foreign monk, the scholar, and the shut-mouthed stillness flat and unmoved.

payload.english: Another was a monk in a yellow robe, with a small bronze ring hung from his ear, of a strangely antique visage at first sight. His skin was dark beyond the common, and, to see the curl of his hair and beard, he seemed a man come from somewhere west of the Congling. For some time he had been patiently flourishing a red-handled fly-whisk to drive off the horseflies and flies that would fasten upon the naked man, but, grown a little tired at last, as it seemed, he had now come beside that same unglazed jar and squatted there ceremoniously, in the attitude of a turkey.
notes: Congling kept as transliterated proper noun; understood as the Onion Range west of China, marking the monk as from the Western Regions. Left for note rather than glossed in text.
Fly-whisk renders shubi: a priestly implement of horsehair with ornamented handle, here red-handled, used to shoo insects. Kept flat, not ennobled.
Like a turkey kept as the low, faintly unflattering comparison it is; not softened.

payload.english: The last stood far apart from the other two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing-yard. This man grew on the tip of his chin, by way of apology, a beard like a rat's tail, and his get-up was a hemp robe long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hung slack. From the careful way he plied from time to time a fan made of white birds' feathers, he was probably a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.
notes: Sobusan and sakattai rendered descriptively as hemp robe and tea-brown sash; the Japanese terms specify plain literati dress, not transliterated here to keep the tableau readable.
White-feather fan kept literal; it is the mark by which this figure will later be known as Sun Sensei, but here the narrator only conjectures scholar.

payload.english: All three alike kept their mouths shut as if by agreement. Nor did they so much as stir, as though they took some uncommon interest in whatever was about to happen, and for that held their breath.

It must have been exactly noon. The dogs too, perhaps sunk in their midday doze, were not heard to bark once. The hemp and millet ringing the threshing-yard shone their green leaves in the sun and stood hushed and perfectly still. And the sky seen beyond them, all stifling heat, trailed a shimmering haze, so that one might have doubted whether even the towering clouds were panting in this drought. Look where one would, nothing seemed to breathe but these three men. And those three kept their silence like the clay images enshrined in the Guandi Temple. . . .
notes: Kept the held tableau in short past stative sentences; rendered Kan-teibyou as Guandi Temple as a proper noun without explaining the deity, and the panting clouds as the narrator's conjecture.

payload.english: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is what happened one summer on the threshing-yard of the Liu family at a place called Changshan in China.
notes: Kept Changshan in pinyin; the text glosses it Chozan.

payload.english: II

The man lying naked in the blazing sun was the master of this threshing-yard, surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the leading men of fortune in Changshan. This man's one indulgence was drink, and from morning on he was scarcely ever parted from the cup. And that, "whenever he drank alone, he finished a whole jar," was a measure beyond ordinary men. Though, as already said, "three hundred mu of fields by the city wall, half planted with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink would burden his estate.
notes: Kept both tags visibly quoted and stiffly quantitative as borrowed Chinese, and left mu and jar unconverted for the pseudo-record measure.

payload.say: Drafted the chess-room interruption and the monk's rumoured cures in the learned deadpan, keeping measures and proper terms unvaried.

payload.english: Why he should be lying naked in the blazing sun has a history behind it, as follows. — That day, as Liu, together with Sun Sensei, his fellow drinker (this is the scholar who had held the white-feather fan), was fighting out a game on the board, leaning against the bamboo wife in a well-aired room, the maidservant came and said, "A monk, lodging they say at Hodoji or somewhere, has just come and insists upon seeing the master. What shall I do?"
notes: bamboo wife: a hollow bolster of woven bamboo leaned upon in summer heat; kept as in the Japanese.
Hodoji: temple name as reported by the maid, hence her "or somewhere"; kept transliterated.

payload.english: "What, Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, and then, raising his fat body that looked hot of itself, ordered, "Then show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It must be that monk, I suppose."

The monk lodging at Hodoji was a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. As he both practised medicine and administered the arts of the bedchamber, his repute stood high in these parts. For instance, rumours all but miraculous were abroad in full force, that Zhang San's black cataract had suddenly taken a turn for the better, that Li Si's byouen had been healed on the spot. — Both men had heard these rumours. With what business could that barbarian monk now have gone out of his way to come to Liu's house? Of course Liu had no recollection at all of having sent to fetch him.
notes: byouen left untranslated: the text does not gloss it and the exact ailment is uncertain, understood only as some disorder of the private parts; no modern diagnosis ventured.
Western Regions, Zhang San, Li Si: kept as transliterated proper terms; Zhang San and Li Si read as stock placeholder names in the reported gossip.

payload.english: Let it be said in passing that Liu was not, by nature, a man who delighted in visitors. But when he already had one guest with him, and a new visitor came, he would generally receive him readily enough. He had what might be called a childish vanity, as if to boast before his guest of having guests. Besides, today's barbarian monk was just now talked of wherever one went. By no means a visitor to be ashamed of meeting. — Liu's motive in proposing to meet him lay much in this direction.
"What can his business be?"
notes: The text names no speaker for p15-p16; the two lines are exchanged between Liu and Sun Sensei, with the second, dismissive surmise most likely Sun Sensei's. I have left the attribution unstated as in the Japanese.

payload.english: "Begging, most likely. He will be asking us to bestow some alms, I suppose."

While the two were talking such matters over, presently there entered, led by the maid, as they looked, a strange-formed monk, tall and with eyes like cut amethysts. He wore a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging heavily, as if a nuisance, over his shoulders. Fly-whisk with its red handle in hand, he planted himself heavily in the middle of the room. He offered no greeting and said not a word.
notes: For the eyes, shisekiryou, I have used cut amethysts for the purple faceted stone; the exact mineral is uncertain.

payload.english: Liu hung back for a while, but as the silence grew somehow uneasy, he ventured, "Have you some business with me?"
At which the barbarian monk said, "You are the one, are you not, who is fond of drink."

"Indeed." The question came so abruptly that Liu gave a vague answer, looking toward Sun Sensei as if seeking rescue. Sun Sensei, with a composed face, went on placing stones on the board by himself. He showed no disposition whatever to take part.

"You are afflicted with a rare disease. Are you aware of it?" The barbarian monk said this as if to press the point. Hearing of a disease, Liu wore a dubious look, stroking the bamboo wife as he did so—
notes: Bamboo wife kept as in the bible: the jointed rattan bolster leaned on in summer heat; the sentence trails in the Japanese into Liu's reply in p22.

payload.english: "A disease— is it?"
"It is."
"No, ever since I was a child . . ." As Liu was about to say something, the barbarian monk cut him off.
"Drink as you may, you never get drunk, do you?"
" . . ." Liu stared hard at the other's face and shut his mouth. In fact, drink as he might, this man had never been drunk.

"That is the proof of the disease," the barbarian monk went on with a faint smile. "There is a wine worm in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not be cured. This poor monk has come to cure your disease."
notes: Kept the monk's humble clerical self-reference as "This poor monk" for 貧道 rather than flattening to "I".

payload.english: "Can it be cured?" Liu let out the words in an uncertain voice before he knew it. And he was ashamed of himself for it.
"It is because it can be cured that I have come."
Then Sun Sensei, who until now had listened in silence to the exchange, suddenly put in a word.
"Will you be using some medicine?"
"No, there will be no need to use anything like medicine," the barbarian monk answered curtly.

Sun Sensei, to begin with, despised the two teachings of Dao and Buddha with scarcely any reason. So even when thrown together with a Daoist priest or a monk, he had very rarely exchanged a word. That he should now suddenly feel moved to speak was wholly because the words "wine worm" had caught his interest; fond of wine himself, on hearing this he had grown a little uneasy lest there be a wine worm in his own belly too. When he heard the barbarian monk's grudging answer, however, he suddenly felt as if he had been made a fool of, so with a slight frown he began once more, in silence as before, to place his stones. And at the same time, inwardly, he thought his host Liu a fool for meeting with so insolent a monk.

payload.say: Drafted p34 to p42 keeping the bare问答 and the schooling aside as written.

payload.english: For his part, Liu of course paid no mind to any such thing.
"Then will you use needles?"
notes: Speakers are unstated here as in the Japanese; taken from what surrounds them to be Liu asking and the monk answering in p35 through p38, left without tags.

payload.english: "What, it is a far simpler matter than that."
"Then is it an incantation?"
"No, nor is it any incantation."

After repeating such exchanges, the barbarian monk briefly explained his cure to them. — According to it, he had only to strip naked and lie still in the sun. To Liu this seemed a very easy thing. If he could be cured by that much, there was nothing better than to be cured. Moreover, without himself knowing it, he was a little moved by curiosity at the point of submitting to the barbarian monk's treatment.

So at last Liu bowed his head from his own side, and it came to his saying, "Then let me ask you to cure me." — There is such a history behind Liu's lying naked in the threshing-yard in the blazing sun.

Then, saying he must not move, the barbarian monk wound Liu's body round and round with thin cord. Then he bade one of the servants bring an unglazed jar filled with wine to Liu's pillow. That Sun Sensei, good friend of the wine mound, should in the course of things have come to stand witness to this strange cure goes without saying.
notes: Kept "good friend of the wine mound" stiff to mark it as a borrowed learned tag, and "thin cord" and "unglazed jar" as in the opening tableau.

payload.english: What sort of thing a wine worm is, what becomes of a man when it is no longer in his belly, what the jar of wine at his pillow is meant for, no one knows but the barbarian monk. Put so, Liu, going out naked into the blazing sun knowing nothing, may seem very heedless, but when ordinary men receive a schooling and the like, in truth they are mostly doing much the same thing.
notes: Kept the schooling comparison as a dry aside in the narrator's cooler voice, as written, without smoothing it into the tale.

payload.english: III

Hot. Sweat welled up prickling on his brow, and no sooner had it beaded than it ran lukewarm toward his eyes. As ill luck would have it, he was bound with thin cord, so of course he could not put out a hand to wipe it away. When he tried moving his neck to turn the sweat from its course, he felt at that instant a violent dizziness coming on, so to his regret he gave up that plan too. Meanwhile the sweat unceremoniously wet his eyelids and ran by the side of his nose and round his mouth to under his chin. Exceedingly nasty.

Until then he had lain with his eyes open, staring hard at the sky scorched white and the hemp field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to run unchecked he had to give even that up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets in the eyes. So with the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, he meekly shut his eyes and lay baking in the sun, and presently he began to feel a certain pain in the skin of every upturned part of him, face or body alike. Over the whole surface of the skin, forces seemed to be at work pulling in every direction, while the skin itself had not a hair of spring to answer them. Everywhere prickled — that perhaps best describes the pain. This was not the misery of merely sweating. Liu began to find it a little hateful that he had taken the barbarian monk's cure.
notes: I was unsure of汗所 in the last lines, which I took as merely being sweaty rather than a clinical term, to keep the sensation flat as the reading asks.

payload.english: Yet, to think it over afterwards, this was still the part that was not so hard to bear. — Presently his throat grew thirsty. Liu too knew the story of how Cao Mengde or someone cured his soldiers of thirst by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But now, however he called to mind the sweet-sour of plums, his thirst was none the less for it. He worked his chin and bit his tongue, but the inside of his mouth still held its heat. Even that would surely have been somewhat easier to bear if it had not been for the unglazed jar at his pillow. From the jar's mouth a thick reek of wine assailed Liu's nose without pause. And, perhaps it was only fancy, but he felt the reek grow stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opened his eyes. Glancing upward with his eyes alone, all that came in sight were the mouth of the jar and perhaps half of its amply bulging body. That was all that came in sight, but at the same time there rose in Liu's imagining the sight of wine brimming undisturbed in the dim interior of the jar, the colour of gold. Before he knew it he licked his cracked lips all round with his dry tongue, but there was no sign at all of spittle welling up. Even his sweat by now had been dried out of him by the sun, and no longer ran as before.
notes: Kept "Cao Mengde or someone" for 曹孟徳か誰か: the vagueness is Liu's half-remembered version of the anecdote, not a doubt about the source.
Kept "with his eyes alone" for 上眼を使って: bound and dizzy from p44, he cannot lift his head and rolls only his eyes toward the jar at his pillow.

payload.say: Drafted the expulsion in flat bodily register with the low animal similes kept plain.

payload.english: Then a fierce dizziness came on, two or three times running. The headache had not let up since some time before. In his heart Liu resented the barbarian monk more and more. And he thought, too, why a man such as himself should have let himself be talked round by such a fellow into bearing such witless suffering. Meanwhile his throat grew thirstier still. His chest turned strangely queasy. He could no longer bear to lie still. At last, resolved, he opened his panting mouth, meaning to ask the barbarian monk at his pillow to call the cure off. —

At that very instant. Liu began to feel some unnameable lump creeping little by little from his chest up toward his throat. At one moment it seemed to writhe like an earthworm, at another to edge itself along little by little like a gecko. In any case, a soft thing, soft as it was, came squirming and pressing its way up the gullet. And at last, when it had forced its way past below the Adam's apple, it suddenly slipped out of the dark, slimy like a loach or something, and flew outwards with force.
With that, from the familiar unglazed jar, there came a faint plip, as of something dropping into the wine.
At that the barbarian monk suddenly lifted the haunches he had settled and began to undo the thin cord wound about Liu's body. The wine worm was out, he said, so Liu might set his mind at rest.

payload.say: Drafted the viewing of the worm and the flat three-year decline without pathos.

payload.english: "Is it out?" Liu said as if groaning, lifting his swimming head, and from mere curiosity, forgetting even his thirst, crawled naked as he was to the side of the jar. At the sight, Sun Sensei too came hurrying toward the two, warding off the sun with his white-feather fan. When all three peered together into the jar, a thing like a small salamander, the colour of its flesh like red mud, was swimming in the wine. It may have been about three sun long. It had a mouth, it had eyes. Somehow, as it swam, it seemed to be drinking the wine. When Liu saw this, his stomach turned suddenly....
notes: Kept "three sun" as a measure without conversion, as the tale measures its marvel; kept the low zoology flat: salamander, mouth, eyes, seeming to drink.

payload.english: IV

The barbarian monk's cure showed itself at once. From that day Liu Dacheng abruptly became unable to drink wine. Now, he says, he dislikes even the smell of it. Yet strangely, from that time Liu's health began little by little to fail. This year makes three years since he spat out the wine worm, and nowhere remains a trace of the round, fat figure of former years. Skin of poor lustre, still oily, wraps the harsh bones of his face, and frost-touched locks linger only faintly above his temples, and there is said to be no counting how many times in the year he now takes to his bed.
notes: Kept the hearsay distance of the decline report; left mu and field phrasing for p54.

payload.english: But it was not Liu's health alone that has failed since then. Liu's fortune too has declined with gathering speed, and now the fields by the city wall, counted at three hundred mu, have for the most part passed into other hands. Liu himself, of necessity, has taken a plough in unpractised hands and lives out his wretched days, day by day.
notes: Kept "three hundred mu" and "fields by the city wall" as quantitative pseudo-record, not converted.

payload.english: Since he spat out the wine worm, why did Liu's health fail? Why did his fortune decline — once the spitting of the wine worm and Liu's later ruin are set side by side as cause and effect, this is a question that readily occurs to anyone. Indeed this question has been repeated by people of every occupation living in Changshan, and from their mouths answers of every kind have been given. The three answers given here are in truth no more than the most representative chosen from among them.
The first answer. The wine worm was Liu's fortune, and not Liu's disease. By chancing to meet an ignorant barbarian monk, he willingly brought about the loss of this heaven-given fortune.
notes: Kept "fortune" for 福 here to hold it apart from "happiness" for 幸福 in the second answer.

payload.english: The second answer. The wine worm was Liu's disease, and not Liu's fortune. For to empty a whole jar at a single drinking is quite beyond what an ordinary man can conceive. Had the wine worm not been removed, Liu must undoubtedly have died before long. Seen in this light, poverty and sickness arriving each in turn should rather be called happiness for Liu.

The third answer. The wine worm was neither Liu's disease nor Liu's fortune. Liu from of old did nothing but drink. If wine were taken away from Liu's life, nothing would remain behind. Seen in this light, Liu is the wine worm, and the wine worm is Liu. Hence Liu's casting off the wine worm was the same as killing himself. That is to say, from the day he became unable to drink, Liu is Liu and yet is not Liu. If Liu himself were already gone, then it is entirely natural, and only to be expected, that the health and fortune of the Liu of former days should have been lost.
notes: Rendered the 即 construction literally and in parallel to keep the third answer's dissolving equation, rather than smoothing it.

payload.say: Drafted the closing refusal and date line in the flat reportorial voice.

payload.english: Which of these answers best hits the mark, I myself do not know. I have done no more than list such moral judgements at the end of this tale, in imitation of the *Didacticism* of the Chinese novelists.
notes: Kept Didacticism in English and italicised as visibly imported, per bible; kept the disavowal flat so the three answers stay equally weighted.

payload.english: Until then he had lain with his eyes open, staring hard at the sky scorched white and the hemp field with its drooping leaves, but once the sweat began to run unchecked he had to give even that up. It was then that Liu learned for the first time that sweat stings when it gets in the eyes. So with the face of a sheep in the slaughterhouse, he meekly shut his eyes and lay baking in the sun, and presently he began to feel a certain pain in the skin of every upturned part of him, face or body alike. Over the whole surface of the skin, forces seemed to be at work pulling in every direction, while the skin itself had not an ounce of elasticity to answer them. Everywhere prickled — that perhaps best describes the pain. This was not the misery of merely sweating. Liu began to find it a little hateful that he had taken the barbarian monk's cure.

payload.english: Yet, to think it over afterwards, this was still the part that was not so hard to bear. — Presently his throat grew thirsty. Liu too knew the story of how Cao Mengde or someone cured his soldiers of thirst by telling them there was a plum grove ahead. But now, however he called to mind the sweet-sour of plums, his thirst was none the less for it. He worked his chin and bit his tongue, but the inside of his mouth still held its heat. Even that would surely have been somewhat easier to bear if it had not been for the unglazed jar at his pillow. From the jar's mouth effect. And, perhaps it was only fancy, but he felt the reek grow stronger with every minute. Thinking at least to look at the jar, Liu opened his eyes. Glancing upward with his eyes alone, all that came in sight were the mouth of the jar and perhaps half of its amply bulging body. That was all that came in sight, but at the same time there rose in Liu's imagining the sight of wine brimming undisturbed in the dim interior of the jar, the colour of gold. Before he knew it he licked his cracked lips all round with his dry tongue, but there was no sign at all of spittle welling up. chapter_summaries.0: Part One. Unbearable summer over roofs, swallows’ nests and drooping hemp and millet. On a threshing-yard at noon three silent motionless men: a fat naked man bound with cord with an unglazed jar at his pillow, a dark-skinned foreign monk in yellow robe shooing flies with a red-handled whisk, a thin-bearded scholar in long robe fanning himself apart under the eaves. Held stillness like clay temple images. Aside: of course this is not Japan but the Liu threshing-yard at Changshan, China.

hard_spots.kind: classical Chinese tags and learned allusion
hard_spots.why_hard: Two quoted tags do documentary work: whenever he drank alone he finished a whole jar, and three hundred mu by the wall half planted with millet. The first measures excess; the second measures wealth. Both sound like quoted Chinese. English must keep them visibly quoted and quantitative, not smooth them into description.

Bamboo wife (chikufujin) to lean on in heat, white-feather fan, long hemp robe with loose sash, jar-measure (u / ichiou), unglazed jar, thin cord (hosobiki). The tale enjoys specifying them. Generic old-China paraphrase would impoverish that scholar’s texture.

Western Regions, west of the Congling, Hodoji temple, yellow robe, bronze earring, turkey-like squat. Period wording (banzo, barbarian monk) marks outsider status functionally. English must neither exoticize into menace nor mute into neutral monk; editor fork on strength of period marking.

Black cataract and byouen (likely genital ailment) cited as instant miraculous cures. Exact modern equivalents are uncertain and unnecessary; English needs plain period-flavoured terms with a note, not a confident clinical diagnosis.

Cao Mengde curing soldiers’ thirst by saying there is a plum grove ahead. Liu knows the bookish trick and finds it useless against real thirst. The joke needs minimal annotation; over-explaining kills the disproportion.

The lump climbs like an earthworm, shifts like a gecko, slips out like a loach; the expelled worm is like a small salamander the colour of red mud, swimming and seeming to drink. Deliberately flat and faintly disgusting. English must not ennoble into grotesque poetry or cool into clinical terms.
Pochiyari, the small splash as something drops into wine in the jar. Tiny sound is the proof of expulsion. Needs a small, unshowy English splash, not a comic plop.
Three hundred mu of fields, three-sun worm, one jar at a sitting. The marvel is measured. Keep measures with minimal help in notes; converting to acres/inches makes it vaguer and more fable-like.
Didacticism appears in English in the Japanese and is part of the closing joke and refusal. It must stay visibly imported and slightly pedantic, not naturalised to moralising.
Gonen shigatsu, April of the fifth year (Taisho 5, 1916). Looks like a classical tale’s colophon and publication marker at once. English must not resolve it into a fuller date than the text gives.

motifs.english: Keep one fixed English term wine worm everywhere, never varied. The ending argues over that single word (disease, fortune, self), so varying it unbuilds the argument.
motifs.why: The creature is at once diagnosis, cure-object and moral counter. The text insists on the same two characters throughout.

motifs.english: Let heat accumulate in the same register: heat, blazing sun, noon, drought, steaming, leaden reflection, burning skin. Do not vary away for elegance; the reader should feel half-roasted before thirst starts.
motifs.motif: heat at noon that will not move
motifs.why: Frame and suffering are both written as weather. Opening tableau, noon stillness and Liu’s burning skin form one continuous scorch.

motifs.english: Keep the same flat stillness wording: shut mouths, no movement, held breath, clay images. Return it emptied in the decline report.
motifs.why: Three men holding silence like temple images sets the tale’s pressure; the same vocabulary of stillness returns as Liu’s emptied life.

motifs.english: Keep jar, wine and smell as a measured set: a jar at a sitting, a jar at the pillow, wine the worm swims in and drinks, smell that thickens by the minute. Do not substitute cup, bottle or alcohol.
motifs.why: Wine is everywhere quantified. The cure uses the same measure as the excess, and the proof swims in it.

motifs.english: Keep the low animals as given, in order, without upgrading: earthworm, gecko, loach for the ascent and exit; small salamander the colour of red mud for the thing in the wine. Their flat oddity is the evidence.
motifs.why: Deliberately unliterary zoology against the bookish frame. The horror and comedy are in the exact lowness.

motifs.english: Keep the three answers formally parallel and equally weighted, increasingly metaphysical, with the third dissolving the first two. Do not make them a crescendo with the third as truth.
motifs.why: Borrowed didactic machinery assembled and left running empty. Parallel form is the point; livelier variation would hide it.

narration.english_tense: Simple past as default for narrated events; keep general truths and the three morals in present. Do not use a historic present for the opening tableau — get its held stillness from short stative past sentences held a beat too long, then narrow to close past-progressive sensation in section three.
narration.frame: Image first, provenance second, explanation third. Held noon tableau with explanation withheld (p2-p7), aside that of course this is not Japan but Changshan China (p8), flashback to chess game interrupted by maid announcing visitor (p11-p42), return to yard for suffering and expulsion (p44-p51), three-year-later report and listed morals with refusal to choose (p53-p59).
narration.narrator: Extradiegetic bookish reteller performing a Chinese strange tale; not a participant. Stages erudite tableau, supplies rumour and back-story, intrudes coolly with an essayist comparison (schooling in p42) and closing Didacticism disclaimer (p59).
narration.person: Third person throughout, with explicit first-person (jibun) only in the closing disavowal in p59
narration.tense_habits: Opening tableau in descriptive present-like literary forms (de aru, te iru); back-story dialogue and treatment preparation in past (ta); bodily suffering in immediate progressive and iterative present-like sensation with past reflection; decline report in resultative past to present state
timeline: Earlier the same summer day: Liu and Mr Sun play go leaning on the bamboo wife; the maid announces the Hodoji monk (p11-p18)
Noon the same day on the Liu threshing-yard: Liu lies naked and bound, monk watches, Mr Sun watches; the worm climbs and drops into the jar (p2-p7, p40-p51)
Three years after the expulsion to the time of telling: Liu cannot bear wine-smell, health and three hundred mu drain away, he ploughs inexpertly day by day (p53-p54)
Time of telling: narrator collects the three current Changshan explanations and declines to choose; dated fifth year fourth month (p55-p60)

part_summaries.summary: Part One. Unbearable summer over roofs, swallows’ nests and drooping hemp and millet. On a threshing-yard at noon three silent motionless men: a fat naked man bound with cord with an unglazed jar at his pillow, a dark-skinned foreign monk in yellow robe shooing flies with a red-handled whisk, a thin-bearded scholar in long robe fanning himself apart under the eaves. Held stillness like clay temple images. Aside: of course this is not Japan but the Liu threshing-yard at Changshan, China.

Part Two. Flashback explanation. The naked man is Liu Dacheng, rich landowner of three hundred mu who drinks a jar at a sitting and never gets drunk. Playing go with fellow drinker Mr Sun, he receives the Hodoji barbarian monk famous for miraculous cures. The monk asks if he likes wine, says he never gets drunk because a wine worm is in his belly, and offers a drugless, needless, charm-less cure: lie naked motionless in the sun. Liu consents, is bound, a jar of wine is set at his pillow, Mr Sun stays to watch.

Part Three. The cure as suffered body. Sweat stings the eyes for the first time, skin prickles without elasticity, thirst grows while wine-smell from the pillow jar thickens by the minute and bookish remedies fail. A soft lump creeps up the gullet like earthworm and gecko and slips out like a loach with a small splash into the jar. The monk unties him saying the worm is out. All three peer in: a three-sun red-mud-coloured salamander-like thing with mouth and eyes swims in the wine seemingly drinking. Liu feels sick.

Part Four. Report three years on. The cure worked at once: Liu cannot drink or bear the smell. Health, colour, hair and estate have drained together; fields mostly in other hands; he ploughs inexpertly. Narrator lists three representative Changshan answers — worm was fortune lost through folly, worm was disease so poverty-with-life is happiness, worm was neither because Liu-minus-wine is nothing so expulsion was self-killing — and says he does not know which is right, imitating Chinese novelists’ Didacticism. Dated fifth year fourth month.

bible.say: A perfect noon cure that is also a slow killing, told in two weathers and refused a moral: keep cure and ruin in one level tone and let the three borrowed answers cancel each other.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Note only what the sentence cannot give: mu and sun as measures, jar-measure, bamboo wife, Congling/Western Regions, Hodoji, byouen uncertainty, plum-grove allusion, Didacticism as imported English. Never note what context supplies or to explain the moral.
style_sheet.author_voice: Young Taisho sinophile performing erudition: kanji-dense, name- and measure-heavy, fond of quoted tags and furigana glosses, dry and faintly disgusting. Learned, not exotic; bookish frame against deliberately low body writing. Guard everywhere against ennoblement into elegance, chinoiserie or wisdom.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Keep the relationship in address: Liu Dacheng on first mention then Liu; the monk as the barbarian monk, never a personal name; Sun Sensei throughout, never Mr Sun alone, because Sensei carries the Confucian status comedy. Keep name order family-first. For Chinese places and names use pinyin in text with Japanese reading in note where the gloss matters (Changshan [text glosses Chozan], Liu Dacheng, Sun Xiansheng), to keep the pseudo-record flavour without inventing readings.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Keep in Japanese with note help only where English has no equivalent doing the same work: mu, sun, hosobiki (thin cord), unglazed jar (suyaki no kame), bamboo wife, white-feather fan. Keep temple and reign-flavoured titles as transliterated proper nouns (Hodoji, Western Regions, Congling). Keep Didacticism in English exactly as the source has it.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese kagikakko for speech and quoted tags become English double quotes; quoted Chinese tags stay quoted and slightly stiff to mark borrowing. No mock-antique thees or ver Cometlys.
style_sheet.register: Learned and slightly bookish for frame and back-story, specifying not smoothing; flat and unliterary for skin, sweat, thirst and nausea. Dry aside voice for the two narrator intrusions (schooling comparison, Didacticism disclaimer). Nobody warmed up; nobody given interiority except sweat, thirst and nausea.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Furigana glosses (swallow, threshing-yard, wine worm, temple and place readings) are reading aids, not double terms; do not carry both into English. Use italics sparingly for quoted Chinese tags and for Didacticism to show it as imported; otherwise roman transliterations in roman type.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the cure's success and the ruin that follows it in the same level tone, and keep the three closing explanations standing side by side, mutually cancelling, with the narrator's admission that he does not know which is right. Do not let diction decide for the reader: the monk must not become a charlatan or a villain in the telling, Liu must not become a cautionary drunk, and the worm must not become a symbol with a settled meaning. The closing word "Didacticism" — in English in the Japanese — is part of the joke and part of the refusal; it should stay visibly imported and slightly pedantic, not be naturalised into "moralising."
crux.point: The story stands or falls on a refusal it performs rather than states: nobody, least of all the narrator, can say whether the wine worm was Liu Dacheng's disease, his fortune, or Liu himself — and the tale is built so that removing it is at once a perfect cure and a slow killing. A rich man who drinks a whole jar at a sitting and never gets drunk is cured, exactly as promised, in a single noon; from that day he cannot bear the smell of wine, and over three years his body, his colour, his three hundred mu of fields and his place in the world drain away together. The ending then offers the three available morals — the worm was his luck and the ignorant monk robbed him of it; the worm was his disease and poverty-with-life is happiness; the worm was neither, because Liu minus wine is nothing, so expelling it was a kind of self-killing — and declines to choose. This is not a puzzle with a hidden answer. It is a Chinese tale, retold from the strange-tale tradition, whose borrowed machinery of moral judgement is assembled at the end, labelled as borrowed, and left running with nothing inside it.
crux.why: Everything in the construction serves this suspension: the treatment is described as therapy and experienced as torture; the expelled creature, three sun long, with mouth and eyes, swims in the jar apparently drinking, and the sight makes Liu sick, not relieved; the narrator intrudes with an essayist's comparisons (ordinary people submitting to schooling do much the same as Liu lying down naked knowing nothing) instead of with verdicts. A fluent English version will be tempted on every page to settle the question — to make the monk sinister, the cure grotesque-but-liberating, the decline pathetic, or the third answer the author's own — and each settling produces a simpler, different story: a fable against drink, a fable against doctors, a fable about genius destroyed.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the two weathers distinct. The scene-setting should be still, pictorial, almost airless — short declarative pressure, the tableau held a beat too long — and then, in the third section, let the English narrow to Liu's skin, eyelids, throat and the smell from the jar, in sentences that follow his sensations as they come rather than summarising them. Do not apply one uniform "vivid" style across both, and do not cool the bodily passage into clinical description.
crux.point: The second thing the translation stands or falls on is that the story is told in two weathers. The frame is a frozen, heat-struck tableau: three men in a threshing-yard at noon, one naked and bound, not moving, not speaking, likened to clay images in a temple, while the narrator withholds the explanation and then supplies it as learned back-story, complete with Chinese names, offices, temples, units of land and rumours of miraculous cures. Inside that frame, the middle section suddenly contracts to one sweating body: sweat running into the eyes and learning, for the first time in a life, that sweat stings; skin prickling as if forces pulled it in every direction while it had no elasticity to answer; thirst worked on by the uninterrupted smell of wine from the jar at his pillow, until something soft climbs the gullet like an earthworm, like a gecko, like a loach, and drops into the wine with a small splash. The comedy and the horror are both in the disproportion — this elaborate, erudite apparatus of a tale, all to stage one man's thirst at noon.
crux.why: This is why the opening must not be hurried into exposition and why the suffering must not be trimmed as repetition. The stillness of the first two sections is what makes the third section's crawling, peristaltic attention to the body land; and the body's reality is what makes the ending's abstract three answers feel so inadequate, which is the point.

open_questions.question: How far to take the narrator's essayistic intrusions — the comparison of Liu's blind submission to ordinary schooling, and the closing invocation of the Chinese novelists' "Didacticism"? The reading allows them as deliberate breaks in the tale's surface, in a cooler, more modern voice than the sinophile scene-setting; but how audible that gear-change is in English — a dry aside or a marked change of register — is an editor's fork. Cutting or softening them would make a smoother folktale and lose the story's actual narrator.
open_questions.why_it_matters: These intrusions are where a 1916 Japanese author shows his hand over his Chinese material; they determine whether the English reader meets a retold tale or a retelling.

open_questions.question: How parallel should the three closing answers be made in English? In the Japanese they are formally matched — "The first answer… The second answer… The third answer…" — and increasingly metaphysical, the third dissolving the distinction the first two argue over ("Liu is the wine worm; the wine worm is Liu"). Keeping the full formal parallelism makes the borrowed didactic machinery visible; varying the formulations would be livelier English and would hide it.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The parallelism is the mechanism of the refusal named in the crux: three equally well-built morals, none endorsed. Ennobling or enlivening any one of them — especially the third, which an English version will want to crown as the true one — tips the ending.

open_questions.question: How to render the monk's foreignness? The text marks it repeatedly and physically — skin exceptionally dark, curled hair and beard, a man apparently from west of the Congling, tall with strange eyes — in the period vocabulary of the exotic ("barbarian monk," a monk from the Western Regions). Whether to keep that period marking at full strength, as what the 1916 text does, or to mute its othering edge in English, needs an editor's decision; the reading is only that his outsider status is functional — only someone from outside both Chinese respectability and the Confucian Mr. Sun's contempt can know about the worm — and should not be converted into mystery or menace the text doesn't supply.
open_questions.why_it_matters: He is the tale's one agent of knowledge, and he explains almost nothing; making him picturesque, sinister or sage-like in English would quietly assign him the moral role the narrator refuses to assign anyone.

open_questions.question: How much of the Chinese material culture to carry over untranslated — the jar-measures of wine, the three hundred mu of fields, the three-sun worm, the bamboo wife Liu leans on at the chess board, titles and temple names? Notes exist for what the sentence cannot give, but several of these are doing quantitative, almost documentary work: the tale measures its marvel. Keeping the measures (with minimal help) preserves its pseudo-record flavour; converting everything to English approximations makes it vaguer and more fable-like than it is.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The exact numbers are part of the strange-tale contract — the impossible thing reported like a fact — and the decline at the end is likewise measured in fields lost and days in bed.

reading.reading:
Begin where the text begins: not with Liu's history but with a held image and a withheld explanation — an unbearable summer, tiled roofs reflecting the sun like lead, swallows' nests that might steam their young alive, every field of hemp and millet drooping, and in the middle of it a naked man bound hand and foot with cord, lying on his back in a threshing-yard, apparently untroubled, with an unglazed jar at his pillow, a foreign monk shooing horseflies off him with a red-handled fly-whisk, and a Confucian scholar standing apart under the eaves, fanning himself and watching. The narrator lets this sit, insists on the silence and the noon stillness, and only then remarks, almost as an aside, that of course this is not Japan: it happened one summer at the Liu family's threshing-yard in Changshan, China. That order — image first, provenance second, explanation third, and the explanation itself a flashback to a chess game interrupted by a servant girl announcing a visitor — is the story's method throughout, and the English must resist rationalising it into a tidier sequence. The strangeness is the architecture.

The register is the second thing to fix before drafting. This is a young Taishō writer performing erudition: a kanji-dense, sinophile literary Japanese, full of Chinese place-names, reign-flavoured detail, furigana glosses and quoted tags ("whenever he drank alone, he finished a whole jar"; "three hundred mu of fields by the city wall, half planted with millet"), written over a Chinese strange tale. The English should feel learned and slightly bookish — a man who has read a great deal of Chinese fiction and is enjoying the fit of it — but it should not tip into period pastiche, mock-antique "thees" and "verilys," or into chinoiserie local colour. The pleasure the text takes in its materials is a scholar's, not a traveller's: names, measures, temples, the bamboo wife against the heat, the white-feather fan. Where the Japanese is dense with specification, the English should specify; impoverishing that texture into generic "old China" atmosphere would flatten exactly what the author is showing off.

Against that bookish frame, keep the body writing in section three as unliterary as it is. The similes there are deliberately low and exact — the thing in Liu's throat creeping like an earthworm, shifting like a gecko, slipping out at last like a loach; the expelled worm like a little salamander the colour of red mud, swimming in the wine and seeming to drink. Do not upgrade these into grotesque poetry, and do not downgrade them into clinical terms; their flat zoological oddity is the tale's evidence. The same flatness should govern the physical details of the frame — the pimple-like smallness of the scholar's rat-tail beard, the monk squatting "like a turkey" beside the jar — comparisons that are a little unflattering and entirely unmoved. Ennoblement, in Berman's sense, is the standing danger everywhere in this text: it wants to be made elegant, exotic or wise, and it is none of those things; it is learned, dry and faintly disgusting.

Watch the repetitions, because the text thinks in them. Heat returns in image after image — sun, drought, steaming nests, leaden roofs, the burning of Liu's upturned skin — and should be allowed to accumulate rather than be varied away; the reader is meant to be half-roasted by the time the thirst begins. Silence and stillness mark the three men at the start and return as the emptied stillness of Liu's decline. Wine is everywhere measured: the jar at a sitting, the jar at the pillow, the wine the worm swims in and drinks. The word for the creature itself, "wine worm," should stay one term, unvaried — not "alcohol parasite" here and "drinking demon" there — because the ending's argument turns on the single word: disease, fortune, or self. Destroying that verbal network, or the sun-rose-and-set regularity of the heat passages, would quietly unbuild the story.

The people should be kept at the distance the narrator keeps them. Liu is fat, good-humoured, small-eyed, vain in a childish way about being seen to receive a famous guest, curious enough to lie down naked on a stranger's say-so, and resentful of the monk only once the suffering starts; he is never introspective and never, even in ruin, presented for pity — the decline is reported almost as local news ("they say there is no counting how many times a year he takes to his bed now"). The monk is blunt to the point of rudeness, answers questions with counter-questions, explains his method only when pressed, and is never given a motive, a doctrine or a backward glance; his brusqueness is information. Mr. Sun, the Confucian chess partner, despises monks and Daoists on principle, speaks only because the words "wine worm" make him anxious about his own belly, and withdraws into his chess stones the moment he feels slighted; his snobbery is the tale's one piece of social comedy and should stay dry rather than broad. Nobody's speech should be warmed up, and nobody should be given the reflective interiority the Japanese pointedly reserves for sweat, thirst and nausea alone.

The fluent failures to guard against, gathered: clarifying what the text leaves open (why the monk came, what the jar was for until the moment it is used, whether anyone is to blame); expanding the Chinese setting into explanation a reader of the tale is trusted to absorb; smoothing the narrator's intrusions — the schooling comparison, the closing "Didacticism" — into the tale's voice; making the ending's three answers into a crescendo with the third as truth; and letting the decline gather pathos. The last pages should read as flatly as a report of weather changing: the man who could drink anything cannot bear the smell of wine; the round body is gone; the fields have passed to other hands; he ploughs, inexpertly, day by day. If the English makes a reader feel instructed, it has failed; if it leaves a reader holding a cured man who is somehow dead, it has worked.
reading.say: Reading delivered: the crux is the story's performed refusal to decide whether the wine worm was Liu's disease, his fortune or himself, with the narration's two weathers — frozen sinophile tableau and contracted bodily ordeal — as the second crux; four open questions (the narrator's intrusions, the parallelism of the three answers, the monk's period foreignness, and how much Chinese material measure to carry over) and three voice takes, the first recommended being the dry sinophile storyteller.

voice_takes.label: The dry sinophile storyteller (recommended)
voice_takes.line: First choice: learned, deadpan, and unmoved — the voice of a man retelling a Chinese record he half believes, whose erudition is real and whose sympathy is withheld until it leaks out only as physical detail. Wrong for it: chinoiserie, archaism, whimsy, or any warmth of moral feeling at the end.

voice_takes.label: The brisk modern ironist
voice_takes.line: Second choice: plainer and faster, letting the absurdity of the noon cure and the pedantry of the three morals read as open satire on doctors, moralists and self-help. This sharpens the schooling aside and the "Didacticism" coda, but risks settling the question the text leaves open — an ironist this brisk will sound as if he knows the monk was a fraud, and the tale's flat, sorrowful last report of fields and sickbeds would have to be played against the grain.

voice_takes.label: The archaic tale-teller
voice_takes.line: Third choice: lean into the strange-tale source with a slightly older English — measured, formulaic, "it is said" — making the piece feel like a translated record from another century. This honours the pseudo-documentary measures and the marvel reported as fact, but in English it easily becomes pastiche, muffles the distinctly 1916 essayistic intrusions, and could make Akutagawa's performance of learning sound like the real antiquity it is imitating.

release.title: 酒虫

casual.en: I
casual.ja: 一

casual.en: It was a heat such as had not been known for years. Wherever one looked, the roof-tiles of the houses, set hard with mud, threw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them seemed, at this rate, likely to steam the chicks and eggs inside them alive where they lay. Still more, every field that was a field, whether hemp or millet, hung its head limply in the reek of the earth, and there was not one thing that, green as it was, was not wilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken with the closeness of these past days, though fair, hung thick and turbid in the air near the ground, and here and there mere shapes of towering cloud, like hail parched in a roasting pan, floated in lumps. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way into the threshing-yard in the blazing sun in such weather.
casual.ja: 近年にない暑さである。どこを見ても、泥で固めた家々の屋根瓦が、鉛のやうに鈍く日の光を反射して、その下に懸けてある燕の巣さへ、この塩梅では中にゐる雛や卵を、そのまゝ蒸殺してしまふかと思はれる。まして、畑と云ふ畑は、麻でも黍でも、皆、土いきれにぐつたりと頭をさげて、何一つ、青いなりに、萎れてゐないものはない。その畑の上に見える空も、この頃の温気に中てられたせいか、地上に近い大気は、晴れながら、どんよりと濁つて、その所々に、霰を炮烙で煎つたやうな、形ばかりの雲の峰が、つぶつぶと浮かんでゐる。――「酒虫」の話は、この陽気に、わざ〳〵炎天の打麦場へ出てゐる、三人の男で始まるのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Strangely, one of them lay naked, on his back upon the bare ground. What was more, for some reason, his hands and his feet were wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself showed no particular sign of minding it. He was a short man, of good colour, somehow giving a sense of dull heaviness, fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stood at this man's pillow, but what was inside that, too, was not to be known.
casual.ja: 不思議な事に、その中の一人は、素裸で、仰向けに地面へ寝ころんでゐる。おまけに、どう云ふ訳だか、細引で、手も足もぐる〳〵巻にされてゐる。が格別当人は、それを苦に病んでゐる容子もない。背の低い、血色の好い、どことなく鈍重と云ふ感じを起させる、豚のやうに肥つた男である。それから手ごろな素焼の瓶が一つ、この男の枕もとに置いてあるが、これも中に何がはいつてゐるのだか、わからない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Another was a monk in a yellow robe, with a small bronze ring hung from his ear, of a strangely antique visage at first sight. His skin was dark beyond the common, and, to see the curl of his hair and beard, he seemed a man come from somewhere west of the Congling. For some time he had been patiently waving a red-handled fly-whisk to drive off the horseflies and flies that would fasten upon the naked man, but, grown a little tired at last, as it seemed, he had now come beside that same unglazed jar and squatted there with pompous self-importance, like a turkey.
casual.ja: もう一人は、黄色い法衣を着て、耳に小さな青銅の環をさげた、一見、象貌の奇古な沙門である。皮膚の色が並はづれて黒い上に、髪や鬚の縮れてゐる所を見ると、どうも葱嶺の西からでも来た人間らしい。これはさつきから根気よく、朱柄の麈尾をふりふり、裸の男にたからうとする虻や蠅を追つてゐたが、流石に少しくたびれたと見えて、今では、例の素焼の瓶の側へ来て、七面鳥のやうな恰好をしながら、勿体らしくしやがんでゐる。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The last stood far apart from the other two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing-yard. This man grew on the tip of his chin, as a mere token, a beard like a rat's tail, and his get-up was a black-cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hung slack. From the careful way he plied from time to time a fan made of white birds' feathers, he was probably a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.
casual.ja: あとの一人は、この二人からずつと離れて、打麦場の隅にある草房の軒下に立つてゐる。この男は、頤の先に、鼠の尻尾のやうな髯を、申訳だけに生やして、踵が隠れる程長い皁布衫に、結目をだらしなく垂らした茶褐帯と云ふ拵へである。白い鳥の羽で製つた団扇を、時々大事さうに使つてゐる容子では、多分、儒者か何かにちがひない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: All three alike kept their mouths shut as if by agreement. Nor did they so much as stir, as though they took some uncommon interest in whatever was about to happen, and for that held their breath.
casual.ja: この三人が三人とも、云ひ合せたやうに、口を噤んでゐる。その上、碌に身動きさへもしない、何か、これから起らうとする事に、非常な興味でも持つてゐて、その為に、皆、息をひそめてゐるのではないかと思はれる。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: It must have been exactly noon. The dogs too, perhaps sunk in their midday doze, were not heard to bark once. The hemp and millet ringing the threshing-yard shone their green leaves in the sun and stood hushed and perfectly still. And the sky seen beyond them, all stifling heat, trailed a shimmering haze, so that one might have doubted whether even the towering clouds were panting in this drought. Look where one would, nothing seemed to breathe but these three men. And those three kept their silence like the clay images enshrined in the Guandi Temple. . . .
casual.ja: 日は正に、亭午であらう。犬も午睡をしてゐるせいか、吠える声一つ聞えない。打麦場を囲んでゐる麻や黍も、青い葉を日に光らせて、ひつそりかんと静まつてゐる。それから、その末に見える空も、一面に、熱くるしく、炎靄をたゞよはせて、雲の峰さへもこの旱に、肩息をついてゐるのかと、疑はれる。見渡した所、息が通つてゐるらしいのは、この三人の男の外にない。さうして、その三人が又、関帝廟に安置してある、泥塑の像のやうに沈黙を守つてゐる。……
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is what happened one summer on the threshing-yard of the Liu family at a place called Changshan in China.
casual.ja: 勿論、日本の話ではない。――支那の長山と云ふ所にある劉氏の打麦場で、或年の夏、起つた出来事である。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: II
casual.ja: 二

casual.en: The man lying naked in the blazing sun was the master of this threshing-yard, surnamed Liu and named Dacheng, one of the leading men of fortune in Changshan. This man's one indulgence was drink, and from morning on he was scarcely ever parted from the cup. And that, "whenever he drank alone, he finished a whole jar," was a capacity beyond ordinary men. Though, as already said, "three hundred mu of fields by the city wall, half planted with millet," so there was not the least fear that drink would burden his estate.
casual.ja: 裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるのは、この打麦場の主人で、姓は劉、名は大成と云ふ、長山では、屈指の素封家の一人である。この男の道楽は、酒を飲む一方で、朝から、殆、盃を離したと云ふ事がない。それも、「独酌する毎に輒、一甕を尽す」と云ふのだから、人並をはづれた酒量である。尤も前にも云つたやうに、「負郭の田三百畝、半は黍を種う」と云ふので、飲の為に家産が累はされるやうな惧は、万々ない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Why he should be lying naked in the blazing sun has a history behind it, as follows. — That day, as Liu, together with Sun Sensei, his fellow drinker (this is the scholar who had held the white-feather fan), was fighting out a game on the board, leaning against the bamboo wife in a well-aired room, the maidservant came and said, "A monk, lodging they say at Hodoji or somewhere, has just come and insists upon seeing the master. What shall I do?"
casual.ja: それが、何故、裸で、炎天に寝ころんでゐるかと云ふと、それには、かう云ふ因縁がある。――その日、劉が、同じ飲仲間の孫先生と一しよに（これが、白羽扇を持つてゐた儒者である。）風通しのいゝ室で、竹婦人に靠れながら、棋局を闘はせてゐると、召使ひの丫鬟が来て、「唯今、宝幢寺とかにゐると云ふ、坊さんが御見えになりまして、是非、御主人に御目にかゝりたいと申しますが、いかゞ致しませう。」と云ふ。
casual.label: house-checked

notes.body: A hollow bolster of woven bamboo, leaned against for coolness in summer heat.

casual.en: "What, Hodoji?" So saying, Liu blinked his small eyes as if dazzled, and then, heaving up his fat body, hot-looking in itself, ordered, "Then show him in here." Then, with a glance at Sun Sensei's face, he added, "It must be that monk, I suppose."
casual.ja: 「なに、宝幢寺？」かう云つて、劉は小さな眼を、まぶしさうに、しばたたいたが、やがて、暑さうに肥つた体を起しながら、「では、こゝへ御通し申せ。」と云ひつけた。それから、孫先生の顔をちよいと見て「大方あの坊主でせう。」とつけ加へた。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: The monk lodging at Hodoji was a barbarian monk come from the Western Regions. As he both practised medicine and administered the arts of the bedchamber, his repute stood high in these parts. For instance, rumours all but miraculous were going round in full force, that Zhang San's black cataract had suddenly taken a turn for the better, that Li Si's byouen had been healed on the spot. — Both men had heard these rumours. With what business could that barbarian monk now have gone out of his way to come to Liu's house? Of course Liu had no recollection at all of having sent to fetch him.
casual.ja: 宝幢寺にゐる坊主と云ふのは、西域から来た蛮僧である。これが、医療も加へれば、房術も施すと云ふので、この界隈では、評判が高い。たとへば、張三の黒内障が、忽、快方に向つたとか、李四の病閹が、即座に平癒したとか、殆、奇蹟に近い噂が盛に行はれてゐるのである。――この噂は、二人とも聞いてゐた。その蛮僧が、今、何の用で、わざわざ、劉の所へ出むいて来たのであらう。勿論、劉の方から、迎へにやつた覚えなどは、全然ない。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: Let it be said in passing that Liu was not, by nature, a man who delighted in visitors. But when he already had one guest with him, and a new visitor came, he would generally receive him readily enough. He had what might be called a childish vanity, as if to boast before his guest of having guests. Besides, today's barbarian monk was just now talked of wherever one went. By no means a visitor to be ashamed of meeting. — Liu's motive in proposing to meet him lay much in this direction.
casual.ja: 序に云つて置くが、劉は、一体、来客を悦ぶやうな男ではない。が、他に一人、来客がある場合に、新来の客が来たとなると、大抵ならば、快く会つてやる。客の手前、客のあるのを自慢するとでも云つたらよささうな、小供らしい虚栄心を持つてゐるからである。それに、今日の蛮僧は、この頃、どこででも評判になつてゐる。決して、会つて恥しいやうな客ではない。――劉が会はうと云ひ出した動機は、大体こんな所にあつたのである。
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "What can his business be?"
casual.ja: 「何の用でせう。」
casual.label: house-checked

casual.en: "Begging, most likely. He will be asking us to bestow some alms, I suppose."
casual.ja: 「まづ、物貰ひですな。信施でもしてくれと云ふのでせう。」

casual.en: While the two were talking such matters over, presently there entered, led by the maidservant, as they looked, a strange-formed monk, tall and with eyes like faceted amethyst. He wore a yellow robe, his grown-out curling hair hanging heavily, as if a nuisance, over his shoulders. Fly-whisk with its red handle in hand, he planted himself heavily in the middle of the room. He offered no greeting and said not a word.
casual.ja: こんな事を、二人で話してゐる内に、やがて、丫鬟の案内で、はいつて来たのを見ると、背の高い、紫石稜のやうな眼をした、異形な沙門である。黄色い法衣を着て、その肩に、縮れた髪の伸びたのを、うるささうに垂らしてゐる。それが、朱柄の麈尾を持つたまゝ、のつそり室のまん中に立つた。挨拶もしなければ、口もきかない。

casual.en: Liu hung back for a while, but as the silence grew somehow uneasy, he ventured, "Have you some business with me?"
casual.ja: 劉は、しばらく、ためらつてゐたが、その内に、それが何となく、不安になつて来たので「何か御用かな。」と訊いて見た。

casual.en: At which the barbarian monk said, "You are the one, are you not, who is fond of drink."
